This is what I think I know from ads on BallyAlley, Astrovision boxes and the like...

When the first promotional pictures of a working keyboard came 0ut from Bally, when they still hoped to have them out several months after the home arcade unit, (aka Home Library Computer) always showed a white unit with the Computer system label. However, they didn't sell units like than until at least a year later.

I'm guessing they were intended to be sold only with the keyboard add under, as a complete system.

However, just before the sale to Astrovision, they did start selling the white units and using the Computer system label for both units.

I'm not sure where/when the Montgomery wards labelled units start, but a large number of white units went there. I have seen white units with the standard dust cover also.

Astrovision advertised the white units on there boxes, so I presume they had a stock of them when they made the boxes.

As the White units have a different ROM from all the other versions, I stand by my presumption that they where a run of units meant to only be sold on top of the add under, but later sold off as the add under was ever slipping/cancelled...

This has never been confirmed or denied by anyone from Bally or DNA.

Lance F. Squire

11512:
While it obviously didn't follow as quickly from my meeting with Ken as I'd hoped, I am happy to say that I finally did get Ken's complete Blue RAM Operating Guide archived. There are a number of complications to doing this with the tools we have now, so it's worth detailing exactly what I did to make it happen.

While some Blue RAM programs just have a single load similar to what you'd see in Astrocade BASIC, the more complicated programs have three loads. The first one has a line to set up where the rest of the data gets loaded, and may contain some data to load into the regular system RAM. The second load is the main code of the program, and is loaded into the RAM expansion. The third load is very short, and sets up some variables.

These loads are sometimes spaced very closely together, which in and of itself can confuse ballybin. Additionally, some of the loads need to be treated differently, as I discovered. Therefore, I used Audacity to break the recording up into three different files. The trickiest one here is the second, which may be much larger than ballybin is used to dealing with. Only the Windows version of ballybin is capable of handling enough data. And this isn't standard BASIC code, so the BASIC load count should be set to zero. The first load is easier to process  in fact the earlier versions can do it as well. But keep in mind that this is treated like BASIC code, so if you use the Windows version, set the BASIC load count to one. This actually had me really confused for a while, because I couldn't figure out why I couldn't reproduce what I'd done with the first part of the guide program on the later parts. The third load, while shorter, is again not BASIC, so BASIC load count should be set to zero.

Doing it this way does mean that I ended up with three separate audio files. I just made a playlist of the files and started it up. Adam was kind enough to loan me his Blue RAM, which made testing much easier. Ken did send me some instructions for loading it into VIPERsoft BASIC.  I had trouble following these because I started having problems consistently doing a warm reset. I believe they should work, however. I'm going to go ahead and upload the program to the group. If anyone tries this, please let me know:

1) Install Vipersoft (call 24576)

2) Type in GET %(!6000);GET %(!8FFC);GET %(!6C20);%(!6C82)=!BF8B;%(!6FFC)=!9000;%(!6FFE)=!C072;BC=128

3) Load the tape using AstroBASIC,as we did for the 2nd part, but this time load all 3 [loads]

4) Now, hold the RESET button down and insert BRB 1.1, using the "Warm-boot" method.

There's a lot of information in the Operating Guide, and some cool animations and the first part, so I hope some people will get the chance to see it.

Now that I've gotten this going, hopefully I can knock out some additional programs from Mike White's compilation tape, which at this point is probably the densest source of unarchived Astrocade programs on the planet. After that, I should be able to fill in some gaps from Ken's collection and the Bob Fabris collection. I've also got some additional material that I worked on while the Blue RANDOM stuff was puzzling me.

Paul

11516:
Paul Thacker wrote:
>>
Loading into the Blue RAM, fortunately, is much easier. Just :INPUT; RUN and the program takes care of the rest.
>>

That's a relief.  The National Semiconductor 8154 chip used in the Blue RAM for I/O has really given us modern-day RAM expansion users problems!  If the chip was easy to get, Ken and Mike could have used it in the Lil' White Ram unit and it could have loaded Blue Ram programs without a fuss.

The cost, in 1977, for this I/O chip was $8.75 per chip in lots of 100 or more.  I didn't realize that the chip was created for National Semiconductors SC/MP and INS8080A microprocessors.  It seems that the chip was used in many other ways.  If you're interested in reading the complete announcement, then you can read it here in the news snippet titled "National Unveils RAM-I/O Chip" in the November 14, 1977 "Computerworld" magazine, here:

http://tinyurl.com/bvtycsx

(or use the full VERY LONG URL:)

http://books.google.com/books?id=5OsHzHowTLIC&pg=PA86&lpg=PA86&dq=national+semiconductor+8154+-datasheet&source=bl&ots=sPUSMOaWMg&sig=JsAqyYLKKn3vm_ls9dm_Y7-O21w&hl=en&ei=0V_mTtySGOWViQLF-rHSCA&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=1&ved=0CDgQ6AEwADgK#v=onepage&q&f=false

The datasheet for this chip is available online at BallyAlley.com, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/INS8154N-Datasheet.pdf

I looked for an FPGA version of the chip, but I couldn't find one.

If MESS ever introduces tape I/O to the Astrocade emulator, it will be very important to get support of the 8154 chip included... but at first I'll settle for ANY tape support in the emulator!

Adam

11518:
While I was managing to not archive Blue RAM programs, I was not in fact resting on my Astrocade laurels. I've continued sorting through the Bob Fabris collection, as well as looking at a few tapes from Ken (though his collection should be a lot easier to deal with now). One major thrust of this was to archive tapes that Bob packed along with supporting papers, so these should be unusually well-documented. As expected, most of these are Arcadian submissions, and I'm finding a large number of unused programs. Who knows  maybe the number of unpublished Arcadian programs will end up rivaling the number of published ones.

Here's a complete list of programs I'm uploading to the FTP site, along with comments when I can think of something.

AstroBASIC:
Atlantis (1984)(Fred Rodney)(2000 baud)(PD).zip
Capture The Dogs (198x)(James Wilcher)(2000 baud).zip  Unpublished Arcadian submission. Your character moves up the screen automatically. Hold left or right on the joystick to move over one square in that direction when it scrolls up, or keep your hand off the joystick to move straight up. Avoid the blocks and try to catch the dogs. You can wrap around from left to right or top to bottom. I was starting to like this game until I found a very frustrating bug, where there is an invisible block on the upper left part of the play screen blocking one of the dogs. Perhaps this is why it wasn't published. It is actually possible to catch them all if you wrap around from the right side at just the right time.
Crazie Dice (1984)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(PD).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Fraction Study (1984)(Fred Rodney)(2000 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Gas Well Bonanza (1984)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(PD).zip
Gas Well Map (1984)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(PD).zip
Koncentration (1984)(Edward Mahoney)(2000 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Math Quiz (1983)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(PD).zip
Nim (1983)(Robert Hilferding and Allen W. Skaggs)(2000 baud)(Mod).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission. Mod of Robert Hilferding's program.
P.T.O. X-mass (198x)(Joe Peoples and Greg Neff)(2000 baud).zip  Unpublished Arcadian submission. I think that PTO stands for parent teacher organization.
Planet Mongo! (1984)(Fred Rodney)(2000 baud).zip  This is one of the best unpublished Arcadian submissions I've seen. It was submitted late in the Arcadian's lifecycle, so maybe it just got lost in the shuffle. Try to track the satellite's movements with the cursor. Don't aim for where it is; aim for where it's going.
Pos. & Neg. Numbers (198x)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Quadron (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(2000 baud)(PD)[a2].zip -The binary files on all of these differ, but I'm not sure about any differences beyond that.
Quadron (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(2000 baud)(PD)[a3].zip
Rotate (1984)(Robert Newman)(2000 baud)(PD).zip
String Loader (1983)(Allen W. Skaggs)(2000 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Telephone Directory or Crypto-Scrambler (1983)(Allen W. Skaggs)(2000 baud).zip  - Unpublished Arcadian submission.  See the audio recordings from Allen Skaggs tape for more information on these submissions. Allen says that he renamed this one to Telephone Directory, but the program still says Crypto-Scrambler.
The Game Of War (1984)(Edward Mahoney)(2000 baud)(PD).zip
Trapshoot #2 (198x)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud).zip - The versions of Trapshoot have different title screens, but I can't tell that the game actually differs.
Trapshoot #3 (198x)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud).zip
Trapshoot (1983)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(PD).zip

Bally BASIC:
Airbrush And Sandblast, Ant Farm (1980)(C. Schreier)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Bally 3 Voice Music Composer, Player (198x)(Jim Dunson, Brett Bilbrey, George Moses, and Bob Weber)(300 baud).zip  Unpublished Arcadian submission.  Jim Dunson modified the music composer program, and used it to compose On Top Of Old Smokey. He included a tutorial.
Bio-rhythms (1980)(Dave Walter and Rich Tietjens)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Compound Interest (1981)(Jess Shadle)(300 baud)(PD).zip
D&D Speedway (1981)(Mario DeLaura)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Graphic Utility Subprograms (Part 1) (1980)(Jim Marselle)(300 baud).zip  These are a number of graphics subroutines, sent in with extensive documentation.
Graphic Utility Subprograms (Part 2) (1980)(Jim Marselle)(300 baud).zip
Graphic Utility Subprograms (Part 3) (1980)(Jim Marselle)(300 baud).zip
Graphic Utility Subprograms (Part 4) (1980)(Jim Marselle)(300 baud).zip
Hamurabi (19xx)(Richard Houser)(300 baud)[p].zip  An early version of the program.
Name Combined With Nicomachus (1980)(Hank Chiuppi and David Ahl)(300 baud)(PD).zip
On Top Of Old Smokey (198x)(Jim Dunson)(300 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Pool (1981)(Bob Hensel)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Pool (1981)(Bob Hensel)(300 baud)[a][b].zip  I found an alternate (probably earlier) version of this program on the tape with the beginning taped over. It's included here in case anyone wants to look at the differences.
Pro Bowl (1982)(Mario DeLaura)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Quadron (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(300 baud)(PD).zip  After playing the 2000 Bd version, this one feels much too slow.
Resequencing (High Address) (1979)(Ron Schweitzer)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Resequencing (Low Address) (1979)(Ron Schweitzer)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Saucer Battle (1979)(John Hurst)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Simple Interest (1981)(Jess Shadle)(300 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Slot Machine (1979)(Bob Mueller)(300 baud)(PD).zip
Space Gauntlet (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(300 baud)[a].zip - The code here is a bit different than the previously archived version.
T-Bone Crash (19xx)(Mario DeLaura)(300 baud).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission. Hold down the trigger to start, then release it at the right time to fall into the car.

For RAM Expansion:
An Education In Mile, Yd, Ft, In, Ton, Lb, Oz, Gal, Qt, Pt, Cup, Floz (198x)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(VIPERsoft or Blue RAM BASIC).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Block Builder (198x)(Ed Horgen)(2000 baud)(VIPERsoft or Blue RAM BASIC).zip - Unpublished Arcadian submission.
Blue RAM Operating Guide (1984)(Ken Lill).zip
Gas Well Bonanza (1984)(Joe Peoples)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC).zip -Only the AstroBASIC version was published.
 H-5 New Walk Figures (1984)(Stanley Kendall)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC).zip - Unpublished program from Ken's collection. Has walking animations.
High Res Bally BASIC (198x)(John Perkins)(2000 baud).zip
Locksmith (198x)(Stanley Kendall and Don Crider)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC)[p].zip - Unpublished program from Ken's collection. An unfinished modification of Don's program. It doesn't recognize the winning condition.
Snare-A-Bear (1984)(Stanley Kendall)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC).zip - Unpublished program from Ken's collection.  Published in AstroBASIC.
Variable Rez BASIC (198x)(John Perkins)(300 baud).zip
ZZZ-UNK (colorful circles) (198x)(possibly Ed Horgen)(2000 baud)(VIPERsoft or Blue RAM BASIC).zip - Unlabeled art program found on Ed's tape.

I tried to archive an unpublished Arcadian submission named Dungeons & Dragons Character Maker & Dice Roller by David Sohinki, but couldn't get it to work. He did submit the source code, however. I also tried to archive a tape of Chicken by Bit Fiddlers, which should've included the unarchived 300 Bd version, but the tape was extremely quiet and wouldn't even come close to working.

Additionally, there are a bunch of scans. I scanned all of Ken's prototype carts. Some of the Action Graphics carts were mislabeled, so that explains any dumps that appear to be missing. I picked up a Creative Computing magazine with an article on Bally BASIC. It has a generally positive view of the cart as an affordable way to introduce people to programming. It includes the program Guess The Number as a short example.

The rest is associated with tapes in the Bob Fabris collection. These tend to be a combination of letters, source code, and instructions. These are mostly self-explanatory, so I won't list everything. One odd slip of paper was found in with a bunch of Jim Dunson papers. It seems to be some instructions for a Space War program I'm unfamiliar with. I'm not sure if this is actually from Jim Dunson. I also decided to scan a few papers mixed in with tapes for a RAM expansion before they disintegrated. One of these had a petrified rubber bands stuck to it, so the scan is partially illegible. I was able to decipher the text by holding it up to the light, and have included a transcription.

On March 26, 2010 I uploaded a disassembly of "Star Battle" in PDF format.  The cartridge was disassembled by, possibly, Tom Woods in 1979.  Yesterday I made a new disassembly using DZ80 and various "Degler" scripts.  I also put some additional time into revealing all the graphics from the game.  Including today's work, I suppose that I put about 10-12 hours into it.  I said that I wouldn't disassembly this game since I don't care for it much... but I wasn't feeling well yesterday, so it gave me something to do.

This new "Star Battle" disassembly is available in text format.  It is ready to assemble with the ZMac assembler and will match 100% with the cartridge ROM.  The cartridge was disassembled from scratch and it was only after it was nearly finished that the PDF version of the disassembly was consulted.  The text version is probably the preferred version for many people, but the PDF does have some additional comments to offer.

You can download the text, ready to assemble, version of "Star Battle" here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/stardis.asm

I've heard some really strange stories about the Astrocade-- but this is one that I just can't even FATHOM.  In 1982 an article appeared in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution newspaper that said that the "Conan" game, which would soon be released for the Astrocade, would "show up soon in coin-operated video games and those transmitted by microwave and cable networks to homes, hotels and other markets, should be ready for the home market through dealers early this summer."

Here is the complete story:


"Video Game Industry Offers Barbaric Spinoff"
By DX Fenten
(Atlanta Journal-Constitution, June 20, 1982)

     Wonder how long it would take someone to figure out how to take advantage of all the hoopla of new movies and convert it into a video game moneymaker?
     The time has come, and experts say it's liable to revolutionize the video game industry.
     The first real-time Dungeons and Dragons-type video game to spin off a currently appearing movie will come to life in homes all around the United States this summer.  Cleverly called Conan, the game comes from the adventure-fantasy character in the Marvel comic book series, which was made into a movie "Conan the Barbarian."
     This video game cartridge, the first to spin off a movie or a comic book, also is the first Dungeons and Dragons-type game that's playable in what is called real time.  This means a player can pick up a hand controller and get right into the action, exploring perilous dungeons, outwitting and slaying assorted monsters, casting magic spells and even confronting some very fearsome wizards - all without having to waste time by typing in instructions.

11538:
Microwave transmission refers to the technology of transmitting information or power by the use of radio waves whose wavelengths are conveniently measured in small numbers of centimeters; these are called microwaves. This part of the radio spectrum ranges across frequencies of roughly 1.0 gigahertz (GHz) to 30 GHz. These correspond to wavelengths from 30 centimeters down to 1.0 cm.
Microwaves are widely used for point-to-point communications because their small wavelength allows conveniently-sized antennas to direct them in narrow beams, which can be pointed directly at the receiving antenna. This allows nearby microwave equipment to use the same frequencies without interfering with each other, as lower frequency radio waves do. Another advantage is that the high frequency of microwaves gives the microwave band a very large information-carrying capacity; the microwave band has a bandwidth 30 times that of all the rest of the radio spectrum below it. A disadvantage is that microwaves are limited to line of sight propagation; they cannot pass around hills or mountains as lower frequency radio waves can.
Microwave radio transmission is commonly used in point-to-point communication systems on the surface of the Earth, in satellite communications, and in deep space radio communications. Other parts of the microwave radio band are used for radars,radio navigation systems, sensor systems, and radio astronomy.
The next higher part of the radio electromagnetic spectrum, where the frequencies are above 30 GHz and below 100 GHz, are called "millimeter waves" because their wavelengths are conveniently measured in millimeters, and their wavelengths range from 10 mm down to 3.0 mm. Radio waves in this band are usually strongly attenuated by the Earthly atmosphere and particles contained in it, especially during wet weather. Also, in wide band of frequencies around 60 GHz, the radio waves are strongly attenuated by molecular oxygen in the atmosphere. The electronic technologies needed in the millimeter wave band are also much more difficult to utilize than those of the microwave band.

Microwave radio relay is a technology for transmitting digital and analog signals, such as long-distance telephone calls, television programs, and computer data, between two locations on a line of sight radio path. In microwave radio relay, radio waves are transmitted between the two locations with directional antennas, forming a fixed radio connection between the two points. Long daisy-chained series of such links form transcontinental telephone and/or television communication systems.

11547:
I'm looking for a way to help automate the disassembly process of Astrocade programs, in particular the graphics (there are already programs to help disasembly the assembly code).

Does anyone know of software that is available for use on other classic systems that would take a raw binary file and create a text file with the graphics shown if the graphics are pointed to?  For instance, in the "ICBM Attack" cartridge, $2BF3 - 2C1F holds the graphic for the "C" in the ""ICBM Attack."  Is there software that would take it and turn it into something like this:

;  Pattern ('C' in ICBM Attack on Title Screen)
L2BF1:  DB      3,15         ; X,Y Size      
        DB      $00,$3F,$C0  ; . . . . . 3 3 3 3 . . .
        DB      $03,$FF,$C0  ; . . . 3 3 3 3 3 3 . . .
        DB      $0F,$FF,$C0  ; . . 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 . . .
        DB      $3F,$C0,$00  ; . 3 3 3 3 . . . . . . .
        DB      $3F,$00,$00  ; . 3 3 3 . . . . . . . .
        DB      $FC,$00,$00  ; 3 3 3 . . . . . . . . .
        DB      $FC,$00,$00  ; 3 3 3 . . . . . . . . .
        DB      $FC,$00,$00  ; 3 3 3 . . . . . . . . .
        DB      $FC,$00,$00  ; 3 3 3 . . . . . . . . .
        DB      $FC,$00,$00  ; 3 3 3 . . . . . . . . .
        DB      $3F,$00,$00  ; . 3 3 3 . . . . . . . .
        DB      $3F,$C0,$00  ; . 3 3 3 3 . . . . . . .
        DB      $0F,$FF,$C0  ; . . 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 . . .
        DB      $03,$FF,$C0  ; . . . 3 3 3 3 3 3 . . .
        DB      $00,$3F,$C0  ; . . . . . 3 3 3 3 . . .

In this instance, the "3" means color 3 (of 4).  This is probably a tall order since color graphics are held in a non-standard format on the Astrocade.  How about something simpler.  For instance, the monochrome large "H-Fighter" Graphic from the "Star Battle" cartridge:

          DB    10000000B,00000010B  ;   X . . . . . . . . . . . . . X .
          DB    10000000B,00000010B  ;   X . . . . . . . . . . . . . X .
          DB    10000000B,00000010B  ;   X . . . . . . . . . . . . . X .
          DB    10000011B,10000010B  ;   X . . . . . X X X . . . . . X .
          DB    11000111B,11000110B  ;   X X . . . X X X X X . . . X X .
          DB    11111111B,11111110B  ;   X X X X X X X X X X X X X X X .
          DB    11111111B,11111110B  ;   X X X X X X X X X X X X X X X .
          DB    11000111B,11000110B  ;   X X . . . X X X X X . . . X X .
          DB    10000011B,10000010B  ;   X . . . . . X X X . . . . . X .
          DB    10000000B,00000010B  ;   X . . . . . . . . . . . . . X .
          DB    10000000B,00000010B  ;   X . . . . . . . . . . . . . X .
          DB    10000000B,00000010B  ;   X . . . . . . . . . . . . . X .

In this a '1' represents a pixel is on and a '0' represents that a pixel is off.

In my mind, if the software was command line based, it would work like this:

DISGRAPH ICBMATK.EXE -C -3 -15 $2BF3 $2C1F

This command line would mean:

   1) "DISGRAPH" is the name of the graphic disassembly program

   2) "ICBMATK.EXE" is the name of the cartridge binary to be disassembled

   3) "-C" means the graphics are in 4-color format

   4) "-3" is the width of the graphic

   5) "-15" is the height of the graphic

   6) "$2BF3" is the address to begin disassembling

   7) "$2C1F" address to end disassembly

Perhaps some software for the Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit or Atari 2600 can create a text file like this.  Does anyone know of software that can help with this graphic disassembly process?

Thanks.

11555:
I had told myself that I wasn't going to stop scanning ("Scan it all!" is my near-impossible dream), yet I think it is worth scanning and OCR'ing (mostly retyping) the description for "Bally's Alley" by John Collins.  The text was all uppercase with no spaces (except between words) and no paragraphs, so it was sort of hard to figure-out what Mr. Collins meant.  The last sentence, for example, I left AS-IS, because I couldn't make sense of it.

I did scan in the program listing of "Bally's Alley" (which was printed out) and one page of memory locations to be loaded after the program is typed (which is hand-written).

Here is the game's description:


Bally's Alley (An Adventure Game)
By John A. Collins

This is the first in a series of adventure programs I hope to write.  This program is a very complicated game.  It may take days, or even weeks to complete.  However it is designed to let you stop at any point in game- break the program- insert a new tape (be sure that it's a new tape so not to destroy the original tape)- type in GOTO 9000- turn the recorder on to record and press GO.  This will make a new tape- relisting of program and present values of the variables restart the game just use the new tape.

When the game starts you will see a menu.  Enter one of the numbers 1, 2, 3, or 4 and press GO.  If you enter 1 you will see a new menu for which directions you can go.  If you had entered 2 you would be able to type in words which may have special meaning like- take keys.  If you had entered 3 it will identify which treasures you are carrying.  You can carry a maximum of 4 treasures at one time.  You get some points for picking up the treasure but they will be subtracted if you do not drop the measures in the right room.  The fourth thing on the menu is the score.  Each room you go into each time will cost you a point.  However the treasures are worth many points so do not be discouraged.  When you see the menu for directions- you can go in one of nine directions (no southeast).

Many times when you enter a location you cannot return in the opposite direction.  Normally there are two directions forward and two directions backwards from a location.  Some of the locations have the same name.  A magic word- sound - color will be helpful.


I think that the game sounds interesting.

@Lance, do you think you might be able to find this in your tape collection?

Adam

Many times when you enter a location you cannot return in the opposite direction.  Normally there are two directions forward and two directions backwards from a location.  Some of the locations have the same name.  A magic word- sound - color will be helpful.



I think that the game sounds interesting.



@Lance, do you think you might be able to find this in your tape collection?



Adam

9000 instead of RUN 9000. The RUN command automatically executes a CLR!
 
Chris

I was curious about how large a 22" x 34" 300dpi color poster would be if I saved it as a TIFF file with LZX compression (which is typical).  It turns out that it is about 170MB.  Saving the TIFF as a jpg with the highest possible quality (still at 300 dpi) gets it down to about 83MB.  Of course, these file sizes are all MUCH too large to download under ordinary circumstances.  So I saved the sample poster as a 150dpi jpg with medium quality.  At that size the test poster still looks quite good and is about 3MB-- which is a VERY managable size.

11569:
Ken Lill sent me an email after I sent him a newspaper article about George Moses from the early eighties.  With his permission, here are some of Ken's comments:


I met [George Moses] at the AstroBash in Michigan [in about 1983]. There were quite a few BIG names there.  Mike White, George Moses, Dale Smith, Rusty Blomeart, Leroy Flamm, Marion Nalapa, and a representative from Astrocade, though I can't remember his name.  (Mike White knows all those who were present).

The day before the bash, Rusty, Dale, George, Mike and Don Gladden (whose house we were at at the time) were all in a trailer behind the house making a production run of the original Sneaky Snake!

We were turning them out about 1 every 3 minutes.  From bare board, programming the EPROMS, soldering them in, applying labels to the carts, assembling the carts, and putting the cart and instructions in a poly-box!
 
Those were the days, my friend, we thought they'd never end!  Hah!
 
Oh blah dee, Oh blah dah, life goes on bra! La la la la life goes on!!
 
Ken

11581:
I'm scanning in letters and postcards that answer some questions that were asked in the Arcadian.  These were sent to Bob Fabris in the summer of 1979.  One of the questions asked an owner's serial number.  When people answered it, quite a few commented that they were on their second or third unit because their first unit(s) failed and had to be sent back to Bally.  Some units seem to have been repaired, while others were completely replaced.  Some people waited months for their units to be returned.  How's THAT for service!?!

The Bally Arcade really was a headache for Bally, and I'm not at all surprised that they got out of the business-- I'm glad that another company kept producing the console.  Astrovision really seemed to get the unit into more people's hands, and their rate of return, while it existed, really did seem to be far below Bally's, what seems like, exchanged service.

If the ROM test shows yours to be a 3164 Arcade, then it's older than any 3159 machine! The mystery lies perhaps in the serial numbers. However, IF what Ken suggests is right, then any real "painted" Arcade would have had a serial number near 41000 and a Franklin Park sticker underneath! All others should be made of genuine White plastic! Note: Look at the real one I photographed. The serial number was in the 43000 range, and it was one of the ones "stockpiled" and sold by Bally. Any Astro Vision White Top would then have to be genuine White plastic, or a phony!

And no, there is no real "age difference" in ANY of the white Arcades! Bally made the original White units (and unless an interview from someone in Garner Iowa shows otherwise) the ONLY white tops! And they were all made before the "Computer System" project was abandoned (in 1978 I believe).

Mike

Hi Adam,

What don't you understand?

The 75361 clock driver is a chip. (See: http://elcodis.com/parts/555252/DS75361N_p3.html for an example of the part)

The location is in the Oscillator Shield (referring to the RF shield over the oscillator).

Describing the failure mode, when the system warms up, this part falls out of specification. Specifically the 'high time' falls below 55ns, meaning the time the signal is high is less that the expected 55ns width.

In layman terms, the clock pulse is shorter than expected by the system, thus causing the system to fail.

Does this help?

Brett

Very few. Most of the failures came from people playing the system on their
carpets, or towels, etc. When the bottom vent holes were blocked, the Data chip
did not get enough circulation and it literally would burn itself up! I had the
opertunity to prove this to one of Chicago's Bally repair station. Rex TV. He
asked me why there were so many returns, and the fixes were these custom chips.
I had him take 2 units home and have his kids play both. One on carpet and the
other on the coffee table. Within a half hour the one on the rug died. The other
survived the entire night.

Ken

One potential investor wants to see the minimum requirements of
turning a game online.   He says there's something to prevent joystick
switches and butons from accidentally actuating, something like a de-
bounce.   He's assuming that you have to hold down a joystick or
button direction for 15 frames in a 60FPS game to actuate a button.
This prevents unwanted noise for accidental presses.  He's assuming
less data can travel or it can be transmitted faster if it doesn't do
it as much.

But I see 2 problems with that.  First, to read the buffer, you have
to know what the de-bounce rate is, and if it;'s software dependent,
you have to read the code, Second it probably matters wether you press
the button between frames 1 and 15 or between 2 and 16, that  60th of
a second could be the difference between a hit or miss.

My question is how many of those 60 frames must something be activated
or decactivated to register, or could you make a Track-N-Field type
game by repeatedly pressing and releasing the trigger or alternating
left and right.  (not that I recommend you do it with an Astrocade
controller, but...) My theory is if a track and field type game can be
made for the Astrocade, then there is no de-bouncing (or at worst de-
bouncing is less than one video frame)and controls are 60 frames per
second.. I guess Color War wouldn't work if you couldn't react in a
60th of a second.

This guy has experience with television monitors for medical display
applications.   I'm don't know if I don't understand his question ofif he doesn't understand the answer.

modified Astro Basic (as did RoadToad, et al...) which is questionable as
fair-useage.
>>

Over the past ten years I've wanted to get the Bally cartridge library
released.  I don't know who owns the rights, nor can I think of anybody that
knows this information.  Instead of releasing the entire first-party
cartridge library, perhaps it would be best to start off with one cartridge,
a cartridge that holds little monetary value, but great value for Astrocade
users: BASIC.  BASIC uses the Bally's On-Board 8K ROM, so without releasing
that ROM, the use of the cartridge would be impossible.  The On-Board ROM
holds two games, which could possibly complicate such a release of the ROM
by whoever owns the rights.

With BASIC and the On-Board ROM freely distributable it would allow hundreds
of Bally/Astrocade programs to be used as well.  Perhaps THEN the MESS
emulator would begin to support cartridge switching and tapes.

Adam

All of Adam's scanning has inspired me to do some scanning of my own. I now only have about a fourth of a box from the Bob Fabris collection unscanned. I found another binder of the ZGRASS documentation. Most of it was identical to the last one, but I did find a more preliminary version of the glossary.

The rest of it is from a big stack of unsorted papers. There is a little bit of everything here, so I won't go through it all. Barry McCleave wrote a letter to the editor detailing his thoughts on a bank switched cartridge.  There is a draft of the introduction Bob Fabris wrote for Bally Alley. George Moses tells Bob Fabris that Bob Weber has released all 45 W&W programs for publication in the Arcadian. Many of these were never actually printed, so we should be on the lookout for the source code of the last couple of unarchived programs. There is a bill of materials from Astrovision breaking down the cost of every single component of the system. There are instructions and source code for Bowling Secretary by New Image. Rich Tietjens wrote a tutorial on random number generation.

I've been following Adam's lead and mostly scanning in grayscale. This does go much faster, because the scans are almost always of good quality.

Paul

11646:
I'm glad that Paul was able to point in the right direction for the docs and
the pictures for the ICBM Attack controller.  Sometimes I think that Paul
may know the Bally Alley website better than I do!

It took YEARS to get a picture of the that ICBM Attack controller.  I still
haven't heard of any game collector that owns one of them (the picture
online at BallyAlley.com is from the collection of one of the people from
Spectre Systems, Marian Nalepa, I think).

Now that it's pointed out, it really isn't obvious how the button layout
works for the game.  While the controller may not have been comfortable to
us back in 1982, this was fairly typical of all the controllers at the time.
I'm not just talking about the worst offenders either.  Even the Atari 2600
controller's joystick, fondly remembered by most people in the classic
gaming community, had many detractors in its day.  It's a safe bet that the
analog controller from Spectre was greeted with open arms, regardless if it
was comfortable to use or not.  It seems that gamers had more patience with
controllers at the time and were willing to forgive discomfort for superior
gameplay-- or ANY gameplay for that matter!

It's great to hear that another person is able to enjoy ICBM Attack using a
modern day controller-- the setup is well worth the small amount of effort
required to get it working properly.

11647:
The keys used for ICBM Attack were the #1, #2, and #3 buttons on the numeric keypad for the left, middle and right bases respectively. Those in combination with the joystick were the controls for ICBM Attack.

We put the 'pinball' buttons on the sides for games like pinball (and they control the left and right flippers.

Hope this helps,
Brett

11652:
What were we thinking? Well, we were a bunch of young kids just trying to have fun...

I wanted a controller that could handle XY movement. A roller ball like they used on "Missile Command" was out of the question. And mice did not exist yet.

I looked at using a light pen, but that made the game too easy. AND you had to sit right in front of the TV.

So I settled on a joystick (Radio Shack used to sell them). I'm not sure why we wanted a keypad instead of a bunch of buttons. Maybe because it was easy to wire into the matrix of the controllers... It is too long ago and I don't remember exactly why we pick it. But the 1, 2, and 3 buttons worked for ICBM Attack and that was good enough...

The controllers were a pain in the ass to build. We had to cut/drill the bakelite boxes, and I even beveled the opening for the Joystick. I could do a much better job today... ;-)

Brett

11664:
The Bally/Astrocade Console and the TOSEC Naming Convention
-----------------------------------------------------------
March 22, 2012
Adam Trionfo


The TOSEC Bally/Astrocade Database is out of date.  This article takes a
close look at where the TOSEC database stands at the moment.  It is hoped
that this examination will lead to the eventual updating of the database.


The "TOSEC" naming convention has been used on the BallyAlley.com website
for about five years, beginning shortly after I brought the subject up in
February of 2007.  When Paul Thacker and I began using it, the naming
standard was a short text document that gave details on how to name files so
that they could be recognized without confusion.  For many years the DOS
naming convention of 8.3 had been used (and sometimes still is, for example,
in MESS), and this made it difficult to know what a ROM was just by looking
at it's filename.

TOSEC is not just a naming standard.  The goal as stated on the TOSEC
website (http://www.tosecdev.org/) is "The Old School Emulation Center
(TOSEC) is a website and retrocomputing initiative dedicated to the
cataloging and preservation of software, firmware and resources for
microcomputers, minicomputers and video game consoles. The main goal of the
project is to catalog and audit all possible kinds of software and firmware
images for these systems."  To this end, in order to recognize individual
files, of any sort, TOSEC uses a file's unique CRC identification.  

Why follow a naming standard at all?  Does it really matter?  To make it
clearer why a better naming convention was needed on Bally Alley, here is an
example.  By simply looking at the filename "mlangman.bin," can you tell
what it is?  Unless you are very familiar with the Bally/Astrocade
cartridges, than you probably can not do it.  The TOSEC name used on
BallyAlley.com is "Machine Language Manager (1982)(The Bit Fiddlers).bin."
The filename contains the full name of the game, the year it was released
and who released it.  That is a simple example, some examples, especially
the archived WAV files used to store BASIC programs on Bally Alley, have
much longer and sophisticated filenames.

It's been a couple of years since I've read the newest version of the TOSEC
naming convention document that I pointed out in 2007.  I can see that it
has grown into a professionally laid-out pdf that contains file naming best
practices.  The file can be read here:

http://tinyurl.com/7jx4624

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.tosecdev.org/index.php/downloads/category/5-tosec-naming-conventi
on?download=19%3Atosec-naming-convention-2011-08-27

The beauty of using this naming convention is that it has caught on around
the world and is used across hundreds of different platforms.  The drawback
is that there is actually an official TOSEC database, and it has to be kept
current.  The Bally/Astrocade version is out of date.  This document aims to
take a close look at where the TOSEC database stands at the moment.


I downloaded the complete, current TOSEC database (which is from February
2012 and is called " TOSEC-v2012-02-29").  I used the database with ROM data
management software called RomVault to recognize as many Bally ROMs as
possible.  The TOSEC database isn't current, which I already suspected
before I started, but the database was able to recognize less than 30
Bally/Astrocade ROMs.  I suspect that these are the ROMs that were online
going back into the nineties.

There are four individual TOSEC dat files for the "Bally Professional Arcade
& Astrocade."  These files are:
 
1) Applications (TOSEC-v2006-01-24_CM).dat

2) Educational (TOSEC-v2006-01-24_CM).dat

3) Firmware (TOSEC-v2006-05-05_CM).dat

4) Games (TOSEC-v2009-10-13_CM).dat

I used these dat files with the most complete Bally/Astrocade ROM
collection, called "astrocade_rom_collection_9-30-2011.zip."  This ROM
collection includes about 30 ROM files that can also be downloaded
individually and it also includes the collection called
"nine_new_dumps_9-23-2011" collection.

The ROM collection from late September 30'th does NOT include any of the
archived programs from tape or the newsletters (which TOSEC dat files
normally include).  This collection was assembled by Paul Thacker and it
includes 117 Bally/Astrocade ROM images and three available On-Board ROM

the ROMs, while the other 98 ROMs went completely unrecognized.

Entering these 98 missing ROM files and the other additional 15 ROMS into
the TOSEC database would be an excellent start to getting the database into
a manageable position.  Even then the database would still lack other ROM
files which can also be downloaded for the Bally/Astrocade that have not
been taken into consideration here.  These other files are scattered mostly
in the BallyAlley.com homebrew area and the Yahoo group file area (most
notable are the BASICarts that Richard has recently been working on).  Also,
the TOSEC database isn't centered only around ROMs.  Other common items
usually included in a console's database are books, instruction manuals,
magazines, newsletters and tapes

By definition, the TOSEC database will always be out-of-date as the
Bally/Astrocade is development is no stagnant.  The best that can be done is
to bring it as up-to-date as possible.  This isn't a small task.  The
initial aim of this article was to provide a guide to know what is lacking
in the database.  I've attained this goal.  From there, it is a matter of
updating the database.

Updating the TOSEC database is not a task that can be done all at once.  To
look at this as a project that can be completed in a weekend would be
overlooking the stamina that is required to keep it going.  The project
requires baby steps, in much the same way as I've worked on the Bally Alley
website.  Looking at the database a piece at a time is the key to making it
a sustainable, fun project.

-- A.T.

Not sure if LOAD was missing or just undocumemted in earlier MESS Debuggers, but it was keeping me from writing a script to load Outpost 19 into Blue Ram Basic 1.1 and run it from a simple batch file.

Now that it works (with one snag) here is/are the required file(s) :

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/ballyalley/files/Outpost 19 BRB.zip


The "READ ME.TXT" covers it all, let me know if it doesn't ...

>>>
This is the Blue Ram Basic 1.1 version of Outpost 19
tape 19 - Public Domain by Mike Peace and Wavemakers


Save all files to the same directory as your copy of
MESS v.142 or higher (with eXtended Memory support).

Note: edit the Current Directory in "Outpost 19.bat"
but do NOT break MESS command line to two short ones.

"Quote marks" are not needed with no embedded spaces
but makes it easier to tell arguments from the data.

Optional: move it onto your Desktop for easy access!


Don't click on script "Outpost 19.cmd", it's not DOS.

Run the .BATch file and close MESS's Debugger window
[the "GO" should have closed it but it won't for me].

Black screen means there's no extra memory allocated
so hit 'TAB', drop down to "Dip Switches" and 'Enter'
then move Right until "16KB Blue RAM Expansion" shows
(4KB is not enough) and 'TAB' again.  Quit MESS now.

Next time you should see the Splash Screen in White,
then the "WAVEMAKERS" logo with animated swooshes and
finally the game itself.  Enjoy the graphics & music.

Eat the Treasures in the order shown for a Big Bonus!
Map Transporter spots & destinations as you find them
and use them to lure the Monster away from next room.


Can't run batch files or type in Command Prompt box?

No problem!  Launch MESS and mount "brbsic11.bin" as
normal, then summon the Debugger with the Apostrophe
key (below 'ESCape') and type "source outpost 19.cmd"
at bottom of the box, and 'Enter' to run the script.



Richard C. Degler,
on or about 4/3/12

No one's really figured out who owns the rights to the system and games.  In 1981, it was taken over by a newly formed private company, Astrovision Inc., which soon changed its name to Astrocade Inc.  They went bankrupt a few years later.  I'm not sure if the rights went back to Bally--I'm not even sure if Astrovision had purchased them outright or merely licensed them.  Alternatively they might have somehow went to Astrocade Inc.'s creditors during liquidation.

Paul

>
> Not sure if LOAD was missing or just undocumemted in earlier MESS Debuggers, but it was keeping me from writing a script to load Outpost 19 into Blue Ram Basic 1.1 and run it from a simple batch file.
>
> Now that it works (with one snag) here is/are the required file(s) :
>
> http://groups.yahoo.com/group/ballyalley/files/Outpost 19 BRB.zip
>
>
> The "READ ME.TXT" covers it all, let me know if it doesn't ...
>
> >>>
> This is the Blue Ram Basic 1.1 version of Outpost 19
> tape 19 - Public Domain by Mike Peace and Wavemakers
>
>
> Save all files to the same directory as your copy of
> MESS v.142 or higher (with eXtended Memory support).
>
> Note: edit the Current Directory in "Outpost 19.bat"
> but do NOT break MESS command line to two short ones.
>
> "Quote marks" are not needed with no embedded spaces
> but makes it easier to tell arguments from the data.
>
> Optional: move it onto your Desktop for easy access!
>
>
> Don't click on script "Outpost 19.cmd", it's not DOS.
>
> Run the .BATch file and close MESS's Debugger window
> [the "GO" should have closed it but it won't for me].
>
> Black screen means there's no extra memory allocated
> so hit 'TAB', drop down to "Dip Switches" and 'Enter'
> then move Right until "16KB Blue RAM Expansion" shows
> (4KB is not enough) and 'TAB' again.  Quit MESS now.
>
> Next time you should see the Splash Screen in White,
> then the "WAVEMAKERS" logo with animated swooshes and
> finally the game itself.  Enjoy the graphics & music.
>
> Eat the Treasures in the order shown for a Big Bonus!
> Map Transporter spots & destinations as you find them
> and use them to lure the Monster away from next room.
>
>
> Can't run batch files or type in Command Prompt box?
>
> No problem!  Launch MESS and mount "brbsic11.bin" as
> normal, then summon the Debugger with the Apostrophe
> key (below 'ESCape') and type "source outpost 19.cmd"
> at bottom of the box, and 'Enter' to run the script.
>
>
>  
> Richard C. Degler,
> on or about 4/3/12
> <<<
>
>
>

> >
> > Thanks, Richard.  The MESS debugger is SO useful when your disassembling.  I

> >
> > If you haven't used the MESS Debugger before, and no nothing about
> > programming, it's still probably worth your time to check it out.  Just try

> > Adam

Mr. Trionfo,

I am a doctoral candidate in history at the University of Delaware where I am working on my dissertation which examine a cultural history of video games in America.  For one of my chapters I have been examining video game hacking, modding, and homebrewing, focusing on the Bally user community of the 1980s as a case study.  I have found your resources at Bally Alley to be instrumental in my research (and the collection was the impetus behind my interest in researching homebrewing).

I have been pouring over your archives of Arcadian, Cursor, and Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter, but I am looking to expand my understanding to get a sense of what different members of the user community thought about the Bally and their role as users.  Do you know if any of the active members of the user community, such as Bob Fabris, George Moses, Don and Peggy Gladden and John Perkins, would be open to interviews?  If so, would you be able to put me in contact with them?    If it would be acceptable to all parties involved, I can offer the transcripts of any interviews for preservation at Bally Alley.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,

Kevin D. Impellizeri, M.A.
Ph.D. Candidate, History
University of Delaware
Newark, DE

11693:
Wow, that is a very interesting dissertation topic.  I think that video games are underappreciated as a part of the culture, perhaps because they're newer than books, movies, and such.  I'll chime in with what I know.  We've had contact with Bob Fabris, Don Gladden, and George Moses, though sometimes not recently. I don't know if they would want to do an interview, but we might be able to get you in touch with them.  I know that Don and Peggy divorced, but I'm not sure where Peggy is now.  Sadly, John Perkins is deceased.  You might also be interested in talking to Ken Lill, Brett Bilbrey, Mike White, Bob Weber, and Dave Ibach.  Ken and Brett are members of this group.  We have a few interviews on-line here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/interviews/interviews.html

There will also be some posts in the (voluminous) group archives.  I've had it on my to-do list for awhile to track down other members of the community. In many cases, I just have a name and a 25-year-old address.  If you do find anyone, or do any interviews, I'd certainly be interested in hearing about it.

Bob Fabris' papers are currently split between myself and Adam Trionfo, with the bulk of them with Adam, since I got all of Bob's tapes.  A number of the documents have been scanned, but aren't yet on Bally Alley.  You could ask Lance Squire about getting early access though the FTP server.

Do you have a working Astrocade and tape interface?  There are all sorts of programs you can try out on-line, as well as some not yet on-line.

Be sure to keep us up to date on your work!

Paul

KEN'S KORNER

THIS  SERIES OF ARTICLES IS TO ADD SOME KNOWLEDGE TO READERS THAT MAY BE IN THE DARK ABOUT  SOME  OF  THE  BASIC  NO-NO'S OF.PROGRAMMING!


 ONE  THING THAT CAN SAVE AN AWFUL LOT OF SPACE IN MAKING PROGRAMS THAT HAVE A LOT OF BOX COMMANDS IS TO MAKE A BOX-MAKING SUB-ROUTINE.
AN EXAMPLE OF WHAT NOT TO DO IS....

100 BOX 0,-65,8,8,1;BOX 0,-63,8,8,2;BOX 0,-61,8,8,3,110;BOX 0,-59,8,8,1;
    BOX 0-,57,8,8,2;BOX 0,-55,8,8,3

THIS CAN BE DONE IN A SUBROUTINE LIKE THIS:

  5 BOX A,B,D,E,F;RETURN
100 A=0;B=-65;C=8;D=8;E=1;GOSUB 5;B=-63;E=2;GOSUB 5
110 B=-61;E=3;GOSUB 5;B=-59;E=1;GOSUB 5;B=-57;E=2;GOSUB 5;B=-55;E=3;GOSUB 5
		
THIS DOESN'T LOOK TO BE SAVING ANY GOOD AMOUNT OF BYTES, BUT IF YOU HAVE QUITE A FEW BOXES WITHIN OTHER LINES, ALL THAT YOU NEED TO DO IS SET THE VARIABLES UP PRIOR TO YOUR.GOING TO THE SUBROUTINE!

THERE ARE TWO OTHER WAYS TO SAVE EVEN MORE BYTES:

 1) IF YOU'LL  NOTICE THE X NUMBERS IN THE COMMANDS ARE THE SAME IN EACH CASE, AS WELL AS THE Y SIZE. THE Y POSITION AND THE COLOR TYPE ARE THE ONLY CHANGES AND THEY BOTH FOLLOW A PATTERN, SO THEY CAN BE USED IN A LOOP, LIKE THIS:..

100 A=0;C=8;D=8;B=-67;FOR F=0TO 1;FOR E=1TO 3;B=B+2;GOSUB 5;NEXT E;NEXT F

THE ABOVE LINE USES UP 49 BYTES. LINE 5 HAS 15 BYTES. THE ORIGINAL LINE USED UP 73.
THAT IS A SAVINGS OF 9 BYTES JUST FOR THE ONE LINE. iF YOU HAVE MULTIPLE LINES WITH DIFFERENT SIZE BOXES, THE SAVINGS CAN BE QUITE SUBSTANTIAL.

2) TO SAVE EVEN MORE BYTES, THE VARIABLES CAN BE PRE-SAVED ONTO TAPE. aSTRO BASIC SAVES ALL VARIABLES. ALL OF THE EXTENDED BASICS CAN ALSO SAVE THEIR VARIABLES TO TAPE.
	TO DO THIS IN THE 300 BAUD BALLY BASIC (#6002), YOU WILL NEED TO DO THIS PROCEDURE:

:PRINT;PRINT "A=0;B=-67;C=0;D=0";:RETURN

THIS WILL INSTRUCT THE BASIC TO LOAD THE VARIABLES AFTER IT LOADS THE BODY OF THE PROGRAM.

NOW THE LINE LOOKS LIKE THIS:

100 FOR F=0TO 1;FOR E=1TO 3;B=B+2;GOSUB 5;NEXT E;NEXT F

THIS SAVES AN ADDITIONAL 18 BYTES. WHEN YOU ONLY HAVE 1800 AS IN THE BALLY AND ASTRO BASICS, THIS SAVINGS CAN HELP GET ALL OF THE PROGRAM YOU WANT.

JUST MAKE SURE THAT YOUR FIRST LINE NUMBER IS LESS THAN 5 AND THAT IT SAYS TO "GOTO" ANY LINE NUMBER GREATER THAN 5!

(Seriously, Adam is running out of space with all the scans he's been making and the scans and recordings I've been making.  But isn't that a good problem to have?)

It's time to upload everything I've been working on recently to the FTP site.  Here are the highlights:

I've made updated versions of prg2txt and txt2prg with two features I've always wanted--adding support in txt2prg for bytes in curly braces, and making prg2txt only optionally look for VIPERSoft BASIC keywords.  I've been using them on a few programs, including a rather complicated version of Rich Tietjens' D&D tape with line numbers packed as bytes and non-character bytes used to signify the beginning of programs.  If anyone wants to look over the code or try out the programs, please pass on any comments/concerns.

There are four new ROMs.  Mike White's tape of programs for the RAM expansion also included some cartridges in tape format.  The only unarchived one I found is a version of Mazeman called Pacmaze. I'm not sure yet if there are any differences beyond the name.  Also, among Ken Lill's tapes, I found three versions of a cart Ken told me he had worked on long ago--a conversion of Golddigger by Dave Carson.  These are very early.  Only one brings up the playfield in MESS, and your character can only move left and right a bit.  Ken thought this was about as far as it advanced.  There are possibly a couple more versions that I haven't gotten to process correctly.

I've uploaded some more audio recordings from the Bob Fabris tapes.  There are a few tape introductions, and then Bob's recordings from an Astrocade Inc. sales meeting.  I uploaded a few of these before, but I've sorted them better now, and added some recordings.  I've included notes on how I think they could be described on Bally Alley.  This could probably have its own subsection on the Astrocade audio page, apart from Bob Fabris' phone calls.  You can check out the agenda of the meeting here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/marketing_materials/pdf/sales_meeting_%281981%29.pdf

I think I've recorded all of the audio tapes now, but it's a chore to get them sorted and described well.

I've scanned all of the remaining folders from my portion of the Bob Fabris documents, leaving only a small stack of loose papers.  I've named the computer folders with the labels of the paper folders they were found in.  There are a number of programs, letters, etc.  There's an unpublished program by Henry Sopko--Missile Defender--along with his descriptions of several of his programs.  There's a disassembly of Muncher.  Robert Newman sent in an amazingly detailed description of his Arcadian submission, Rotate.

Finally, there are still more tape programs.  It is amazing how many of these people made, isn't it?

100 BOX 0,-65,8,8,1;BOX 0,-63,8,8,2;BOX 0,-61,8,8,3,110;BOX 0,-59,8,8,1;

BOX 0-,57,8,8,2;BOX 0,-55,8,8,3



THIS CAN BE DONE IN A SUBROUTINE LIKE THIS:



5 BOX A,B,D,E,F;RETURN

100 A=0;B=-65;C=8;D=8;E=1;GOSUB 5;B=-63;E=2;GOSUB 5

110 B=-61;E=3;GOSUB 5;B=-59;E=1;GOSUB 5;B=-57;E=2;GOSUB 5;B=-55;E=3;GOSUB 5



THIS DOESN'T LOOK TO BE SAVING ANY GOOD AMOUNT OF BYTES, BUT IF YOU HAVE

QUITE A FEW BOXES WITHIN OTHER LINES, ALL THAT YOU NEED TO DO IS SET THE

VARIABLES UP PRIOR TO YOUR.GOING TO THE SUBROUTINE!



THERE ARE TWO OTHER WAYS TO SAVE EVEN MORE BYTES:



1) IF YOU'LL NOTICE THE X NUMBERS IN THE COMMANDS ARE THE SAME IN EACH CASE,

AS WELL AS THE Y SIZE. THE Y POSITION AND THE COLOR TYPE ARE THE ONLY

CHANGES AND THEY BOTH FOLLOW A PATTERN, SO THEY CAN BE USED IN A LOOP, LIKE

THIS:..



100 A=0;C=8;D=8;B=-67;FOR F=0TO 1;FOR E=1TO 3;B=B+2;GOSUB 5;NEXT E;NEXT F



THE ABOVE LINE USES UP 49 BYTES. LINE 5 HAS 15 BYTES. THE ORIGINAL LINE USED

UP 73.

THAT IS A SAVINGS OF 9 BYTES JUST FOR THE ONE LINE. iF YOU HAVE MULTIPLE

LINES WITH DIFFERENT SIZE BOXES, THE SAVINGS CAN BE QUITE SUBSTANTIAL.



2) TO SAVE EVEN MORE BYTES, THE VARIABLES CAN BE PRE-SAVED ONTO TAPE. aSTRO

BASIC SAVES ALL VARIABLES. ALL OF THE EXTENDED BASICS CAN ALSO SAVE THEIR

VARIABLES TO TAPE.

TO DO THIS IN THE 300 BAUD BALLY BASIC (#6002), YOU WILL NEED TO DO THIS

PROCEDURE:



:PRINT;PRINT "A=0;B=-67;C=0;D=0";:RETURN



THIS WILL INSTRUCT THE BASIC TO LOAD THE VARIABLES AFTER IT LOADS THE BODY

OF THE PROGRAM.



NOW THE LINE LOOKS LIKE THIS:



100 FOR F=0TO 1;FOR E=1TO 3;B=B+2;GOSUB 5;NEXT E;NEXT F



THIS SAVES AN ADDITIONAL 18 BYTES. WHEN YOU ONLY HAVE 1800 AS IN THE BALLY

AND ASTRO BASICS, THIS SAVINGS CAN HELP GET ALL OF THE PROGRAM YOU WANT.



JUST MAKE SURE THAT YOUR FIRST LINE NUMBER IS LESS THAN 5 AND THAT IT SAYS

TO "GOTO" ANY LINE NUMBER GREATER THAN 5!

11713:
If something IS working and then stops working after the Bally/Astrocade is
on for a short while, then you can bet the console is overheating.  Since
your problem is very specific (only the knobs-- the pots), then it is
probably the I/O chip.  The custom I/O chip  reads the pots through the
Analog-Digital Converter circuit that is contained within it.  However, even
if the I/O chip is defective, then since it has already overheated, then the
system may have other problems too.  There WAS a source up until at least
2011 where a Bally I/O chip could be had for about $40 (yes, expensive), but
it doesn't seem to be available anymore from this source.  For more
information on this, see message #10849 and the postings that follow it.

It's possible that using the Astrocade without the shielding and the plastic
cover will keep it from overheating and the custom I/O may keep
functioning-- but even if this "fix" DOES work, then it's a marginal system
that will likely eventually fail.  However, removing the shielding should
always be done anyway on ALL units, so it's worth a try to see if this has
any effect at all.

If you have a spare "dead" Bally/Astrocade around, then you may consider
just swapping the I/O chips, as the chip is socketed and is easy to remove.
The only trouble here is if that spare I/O chip is bad too, then you're not
going to learn anything new.  Still, if it doesn't cost you anything, then
I'd say it is worth trying.  The I/O chip is labeled U19 on the PCB Board
Layout of the Bally Service Manual (see page 24).  Here is a link to the
manual:

http://tinyurl.com/ycmv7em

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/misc_hardware_docs/Bally/full_size/b
ally_service_manual.pdf

I hope that this helps.

Adam

11716:
My lack of plans Saturday was somewhat boring for me, but very good for Astrocade archiving.  I've now scanned the last of my documents from Bob Fabris' collection, and uploaded them to the FTP server.  These were a bunch of loose papers, so there was a little bit of everything mixed in there.  It did include some of the more interesting documents I've found there.

An amusing rejected Arcadian submission is "Playboy Bunny" by Drew Davidson.  I guess the Arcadian just wasn't that kind of magazine.  Or maybe it was as much because the program wasn't that interesting.  I actually think I might be missing the end of it.  The page I have just seems to print out "Playboy Bunny" a bunch of times.  Adam--let me know if you run across any steamy BASIC code in your papers.  There were a few other programs, including Life IV by Matt Giwer.

I found a lot of letters that JS&A sent to their customers.  Bob was obviously upset with them, and even marked up some of their ads detailing the inaccuracies, to send to magazines that carried the ads.  (By the way, Bob stated that the first systems arrived January 1978.)  In JS&A's defense, it seems to me that a lot of the delays and unmet promises came more from Bally's end.  JS&A certainly offered more compensation to their customers than they were required to do, including letting purchasers return the system for credit when, about a year after it was sold, it became apparent that Bally would not be releasing the keyboard expansion anytime soon.  However, JS&A admitted that they were too trusting of Bally's claims and timeframe, and didn't adequately inform their customers during the delays.  And once JS&A dropped the product, they didn't try to keep the people who purchased one informed about the system.  Bob asked JS&A if he could get a list of people to send information about the Arcadian to, and JS&A replied that giving out such information was against their policies.  I do understand this, but it would have been a nice gesture to send a note to their customers letting them know that there was a user community out there.  After all, this was before they could just Google it.

I learned that Larry Camnitz was originally planning to sell The Dragon and Vegas 500 (two tape programs that Adam and I found in tape and paper format).  It appears these plans were scuttled after it was going to get a rather negative review.  I don't find the programs particularly exciting, but they are at least a unique take on largely chance-based games.  I certainly prefer them to the umpteen versions of slot machine.

There is some correspondence between Bob and some people you might be familiar with--Fred Cornett, Brett Bilbrey, Karen Nelson, Dave Ibach, and Guy McLimore. I also thought some of the letters from less well known subscribers were interesting.  Hope and disappointment over the keyboard expansion was a common theme.  I particularly liked the letter from Dick Belton detailing his attempts to contact Bally about the expansion, and also talking to Bob about the struggles of trying to run the Maryland users group.  He included a copy of one of their newsletters, which is the first of these I've ever run across.  (And quite possibly, the only one still extant.)

Well, that's all I've got, so I guess I'll be concentrating (even more) on tape programs in the immediate future.  I've actually recorded most of the tapes now, but the real effort is in processing and testing them.  But given how many documents there are between Adam and myself, I'm sure they'll be going onto the website for some time to come.

Paul

My lack of plans Saturday was somewhat boring for me, but very good for
Astrocade archiving. I've now scanned the last of my documents from Bob
Fabris' collection, and uploaded them to the FTP server. These were a bunch
of loose papers, so there was a little bit of everything mixed in there. It
did include some of the more interesting documents I've found there.

An amusing rejected Arcadian submission is "Playboy Bunny" by Drew Davidson.
I guess the Arcadian just wasn't that kind of magazine. Or maybe it was as
much because the program wasn't that interesting. I actually think I might
be missing the end of it. The page I have just seems to print out "Playboy
Bunny" a bunch of times. Adam--let me know if you run across any steamy
BASIC code in your papers. There were a few other programs, including Life
IV by Matt Giwer.

I found a lot of letters that JS&A sent to their customers. Bob was
obviously upset with them, and even marked up some of their ads detailing
the inaccuracies, to send to magazines that carried the ads. (By the way,
Bob stated that the first systems arrived January 1978.) In JS&A's defense,
it seems to me that a lot of the delays and unmet promises came more from
Bally's end. JS&A certainly offered more compensation to their customers
than they were required to do, including letting purchasers return the
system for credit when, about a year after it was sold, it became apparent
that Bally would not be releasing the keyboard expansion anytime soon.
However, JS&A admitted that they were too trusting of Bally's claims and
timeframe, and didn't adequately inform their customers during the delays.
And once JS&A dropped the product, they didn't try to keep the people who
purchased one informed about the system. Bob asked JS&A if he could get a
list of people to send information about the Arcadian to, and JS&A replied
that giving out such information was against their policies. I do understand
this, but it would have been a nice gesture to send a note to their
customers letting them know that there was a user community out there. After
all, this was before they could just Google it.

I learned that Larry Camnitz was originally planning to sell The Dragon and
Vegas 500 (two tape programs that Adam and I found in tape and paper
format). It appears these plans were scuttled after it was going to get a
rather negative review. I don't find the programs particularly exciting, but
they are at least a unique take on largely chance-based games. I certainly
prefer them to the umpteen versions of slot machine.

There is some correspondence between Bob and some people you might be
familiar with--Fred Cornett, Brett Bilbrey, Karen Nelson, Dave Ibach, and
Guy McLimore. I also thought some of the letters from less well known
subscribers were interesting. Hope and disappointment over the keyboard
expansion was a common theme. I particularly liked the letter from Dick
Belton detailing his attempts to contact Bally about the expansion, and also
talking to Bob about the struggles of trying to run the Maryland users
group. He included a copy of one of their newsletters, which is the first of
these I've ever run across. (And quite possibly, the only one still extant.)

Well, that's all I've got, so I guess I'll be concentrating (even more) on
tape programs in the immediate future. I've actually recorded most of the
tapes now, but the real effort is in processing and testing them. But given
how many documents there are between Adam and myself, I'm sure they'll be
going onto the website for some time to come.

Paul

While Brett doesn't list HIS favorite video, I'll bet it's "Treasure..."
something?  My fave game, "Dog Patch," is listed, but most of the list is
made of great games.  I probably don't have to point those out, but there
are some pretty bad games in there too.  There are four that REALLY struck
me and I'm going to call them out:

1) Grand Prix / Demolition Derby - This is probably the best of the worst of
this list.

2) Letter Match - This game isn't bad through any fault of its own, it's
just not quite aimed at my age bracket.

3) Seawolf / Missile - This is one of the VERY few Astrocade games that
doesn't have smooth graphics.  It's an early one, but that's not an excuse.
Gunfight is early and it's movement is silky smooth.  The game itself isn't
TERRIBLE, but, like MANY games, neither of these two games (which might as
well be the same, but backward) has stood the test of time.

4) Star Battle - I was playing this a few months back and the game isn't
quite as bad as I've always thought.  That's not to say that it's a GOOD
game.  The problem here is that the controls, for such a simple game, are
not intuitive at all.

There is a link on the video page to the Astrocade reviews.  There is a
summary of game reviews there, which, strangely, doesn't seem to have all
the games in the videos (but it DOES have additional games).  Each of the
following games do get full review (well, a paragraph or two, anyway).  The
ratings of the games are:

1) Amazing Maze - C+
2) Astro Battle - B-
3) Bally Pin - B+
4) Blackjack, Poker, and Acey Deucey - D-
5) Clowns/Brickyard - B
6) Crazy Climber	 - B
7) Dog Patch - B
8) Football - D
9) Galactic Invasion - A-
10) Grand Prix - C-
11) Gunfight - B
12) Incredible Wizard, The - A
13) Letter Match/Spell 'N Score/Crosswords - C
14) Muncher - A
15) Pirate's Chase - D
16) Red Baron/Panzer Attack - C-
17) Solar Conqueror - B-
18) Space Fortress - D-
19) Star Battle - F-
20) Tornado Baseball, Tennis, Hockey, and Handball - C-
21) Treasure Cove - B
22) Zzzap and Dodgem - F

"Star Battle" scores very poorly, with an F-Minus!  I guess it doesn't get
worse than that!  "Treasure Cove" gets a good review, here:

http://videogamecritic.net/astromz.htm#Pirate%27s_Chase

People always love that game's title screen (and, really, who can blame
them?).

Thanks for the link, Brett.

Adam

real Astrocades and the MESS emulator doesn't support the tapes.

Anyone else have a favorite Astrocade game that didn't make the cut?

11727:
Michael Di Salvo wrote:
>>
I remember reading that this was a Mike White hack, I'm just wondering why
he chose to use that specific configuration instead of just using the
joystick (like Atari did with Missle Command).
>>

I think Mike choose this method because he was having trouble finding the
controller routine(s) for the original version.  Remember, that this was
before easy access to disassemblers and other programs that would have made
this much easier for him.  As for not using the original Missile Command
configuration, I think that Brett talked about this once.  There is a
prototype version of the cart that loads into BASIC via :RUN (it IS a
machine language program).  That version of the game, I THINK, uses regular
controls, but Brett decided not to go with that-- and I'm very glad.  While
Missile Command on the Atari 2600 DOES work (pretty well, I might add), it
doesn't compare to the arcade original and I believe Brett was aiming for a
control method like that.  Any comments, Brett?

>>
Any thoughts on my trackball question/suggestion?
>>

As for using the Atari trackball controller on the Astrocade.  It would have
to be rewired to use two hand controller ports on the Astrocade-- just as
the ICBM controller uses two ports.  In addition, the pots are different, so
those would have to be changed too.  I'm not sure if you've ever used the
trackball controller in trackball mode, but it doesn't work as well as, say,
the arcade version of Missile Command.  Then again, I guess you can't expect
it to work that well.  In the early 1980's that controller was rather
inexpensive.  I think I got my first one at Kay-Bee toys in about 1985/85
for $5 (the same day I also got two Amiga joysticks-- it was a good
controller day!).  I'm not sure how much the trackball controller cost when
first released.  Anyone know?  I used to use the controller in joystick mode
on my C64 when I played Centipede and it made the game VASTLY better, but
the fire button was awkward.  I can't recall which game I used the
trackball's trackball-mode on (I think it was a 2600 homebrew game), but it
didn't control nearly as good as I expected.

Adam

11732:
I added the manual for the 1978 VideoBrain "Timeshare" communications cart
(#CM01).  This manual was already turned into a pdf by Lance and uploaded to
his site on January 12, 2012.  His version is about 4MB, compared with this
8MB version.  This new version has also been cleaned-up a bit.

Here is some additional information taken from the "Timeshare" manual's
introduction:


"This program cartridge converts your VideoBrain into a timeshare terminal.
Now you can 'access' the data banks and computer power of a large timeshare
system over telephone lines- to learn the Dow Jones index, for example.
Timeshare can communicate with all computers that allow remote
(telephone-linked) access."

"Teamed with the VideoBrain Expander 1 and 2, Time-share sends and receives
data using the US ASCII code system."

"This manual describes the installation, checkout and operating procedures
for using your VideoBrain as a timeshare terminal. In addition, an
introductory section provides a conceptual view of timesharing."


You can view the "Timeshare" manuals as a pdf, here:


http://tinyurl.com/6pszlso

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.orphanedgames.com/videobrain/manuals/Timeshare/Timeshare%20(1978)
(VideoBrain).pdf


The last few VideoBrain manuals that I've added to the VideoBrain website
have been converted into RTF files.  I chose not to do that with the
"Timeshare" manual because a VERY large portion of it would not be able to
OCR; most of the manual is pictures.

VideoBrain seems to have offered this manual for sale separately from the
program cartridge.  At least that was probably their intent-- the manual's
front page says that it costs five dollars.

Have fun!

Adam

11738:
>>
That's a fun story in the article about getting online.
>>

Yeah, it is pretty funny.  This story has always stuck out in my head
because the last system one might expect to find online in 1980 was the
Bally Arcade.  It's really no surprise that when the person(s) on The Source
"discovered [the Bally group] were communicating via a Bally Arcade, [the
Bally Group] read across the screen, "YOU'VE OT TO BE KIDDING."

>>
Has anyone ever seen an Astrocade modem?
>>

I think that I remember Mike White saying that only three of these were
made.  At least three that worked with the Astrocade-- they were probably a
Hayes-compatible modem that had a hacked interface.

>>
I actually have a tape from Perkins Engineering with a modem driver.
>>

That's unexpected.  I always thought that the Blue Ram Utility 3 was used
for the modem.  The Utility DOES have two commands built into it: Send and
Receive.  From the Blue Ram Utility 3 manual:

"SEND - Sends a block of data over the telephone to another Blue Ram (via an
optional modem interface and modem).

RECV - Receives a block of data sent over the telephone from another Blue
Ram (via the option modem interface and modem).

"These two commands transfer programs or other data between Blue Rams. The
first step is to call the other party. Set your modem to originate frequency
and full duplex mode. The other party should use answer frequency and full
duplex mode. Communications are read when the Carrier Detect (CD) light is
lit on your modems. Once this happens set tape switch to save and execute
the SEND and RECV commands. The party receiving data must execute the RECV
command prior to execution of the SEND command by the other party."


The full "Blue Ram Utility" manual can be read here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/docs-blue_ram_utility3.pdf

Paul, you've used the utility before, right?  Someone needs to make a video
of this program in use.  It's certainly one of the most advanced and useful
programs on the Bally Astrocade.  Ken Lill still uses it to this day on a
semi-regular basis.

>>
is there any service still running that would be compatible [the Bally
modem]?
>>

I would suppose that if the modem was ASCII compatible (much like
"TimeShare" on the Videobrain does require).  Even if there is a system that
still supports either of these programs, it's quite likely that those
systems don't support 300-BAUD.  If either the Bally or the VideoBrain was
connecting to a system, then you'd hear the modems communicating while they
negotiate a speed (you know, that typical racket that modems make when they
first start up).  Once the system realizes that the Bally or Videocade can't
communicate at a higher speed then it disconnects automatically.  For the
VideoBrain this speed can be set to 110-Baud or 300-Baud.  I'm not sure what
the limitation of the Astrocade was for serial communication.

It was fairly typical by the mid-nineties that a BBS wouldn't communicate
slower than 2,400-BAUD, and some cut that off at 14,400-BAUD.  That's
because, whoever is running the service doesn't want a line tied up to such
a slow modem when someone else probably requires it.  A fairly typical local
BBS had 2-5 lines.  The largest BBS in my area (Albuquerque) had far more
lines then other typically did (I think it was 20 lines).  I met this SYSOP
years later and his phone bill everyone month was well above $1,000.  That's
why local a local BBS with more than a few lines charged users just like the
larger information services.  I recall at least one BBS in town that closed
because the SYSOP couldn't pay the phone bill.

It was also fairly typical until the early-to-mid 1990's for services to
charge more money for a user to use the higher-speed modems.  This was
because the service typically had less of them and so using them really WAS
a premium.  When I would download from the Atari Roundtable on GEnie, I
would use 2,400-Baud while reading, but then I would typically use 9,600
baud (the fast my Atari could communicate before dropping character) to
download files (speeds could be changed while accessing the service without
hanging up).  The more expensive 9,600 rate would be balanced out by the
faster download speed.  It was also very important for me to save to my RAM
disk, as using the disk drive was slow and I would still be connected at the
faster rate while my drive saved and nothing downloaded at all.

I tell ya, the Internet sure is a lot more user-friendly nowadays!

Does anyone else remember these times?

Adam
