11743:
Hi Kevin,

I watched your presentation "Homebrewing & Video Games". I'm curious, what created your interest in the Bally in the first place?



While the Bally was not 'successful', an unintended outcome of the Bally Arcade was creating an interest for me in video games. Which led me down the electronic engineering path, and eventually, my employment at Apple. I'm currently heading up Apple's technology advancement group, and my team have created many Apple products. I would not have ended up here if it had not been for the Bally Arcade.

With respect to the 'Arcade market' crash in 1983/1984, my personal option is that the crash occurred because the pinball and video game market was over sold. That is, The major game manufactures were selling to arcades (which were VERY popular back then), and arcades were selling their 'older' machines to secondary markets (convenience stores, entrance of K-marts, Walmarts, and other popular places), and the secondary market was selling their games to the 'home' market. Well, the home market which was buying used games became saturated and stopped buying from the secondary market. The secondary market not being able to get rid of their older machines stopped buying from Arcades, and that made it harder for Arcades to 'turn over' machines and they slowed down buying new arcade machines. And that is what I feel led to the 'game market crash'.

George Moses and Don Gladden were very much the heart of the Michigan Bally Users Group. And George even went as far as working with Bally to write the Basic Manual update when the update to the Basic cartridge was released. But George did not write the music 'player', he used my music code, and wrote his music programs based on that. George was not a machine language programmer... Scott Noris was the person that programmed the 'music maker' cartridge.

Before there was a "ZGRASS VIPER", there was a Datamax UV-1 ZGRASS machine that was used by Bally for game development (both for the home arcade, and their commercial games. I used on briefly.

Anyway, interesting how history sees the old Bally/Astrocade days. It was a different thing all together to live through it... ;-)

The discussion that followed your "homebrewing" presentation was interesting, the discussion of 'hacking products' (including the iPhone and iPad). Obviously, I can't discuss details pertaining to that, but it was interesting seeing the perspective from your audience.

I smiled at the discussion about 'communications prior to the internet'. It was harder to make contacts back then, which is why 'gatherings' were more popular. It was all we had at the time. ;-)

As to lawsuits about copyright infringement, there was little interest from the big guys to sue the 'cottage industry'. Why? Because to sue someone, you expect to get money from them, and the hobbyists that were making copies of video games were not making much money at all. Certainly not enough to sue them over... Any lawsuits were simply done when the hobbyists crossed the line and it became a piracy problem, that is when a hobbyist tried to make enough money that it cut into the profits of the big guys.

Oh how things have changed.

All in all, an interesting discussion...
Brett

> With respect to the 'Arcade market' crash in 1983/1984, my personal option is that the crash occurred because the pinball and video game market was over sold. That is, The major game manufactures were selling to arcades (which were VERY popular back then), and arcades were selling their 'older' machines to secondary markets (convenience stores, entrance of K-marts, Walmarts, and other popular places), and the secondary market was selling their games to the 'home' market. Well, the home market which was buying used games became saturated and stopped buying from the secondary market. The secondary market not being able to get rid of their older machines stopped buying from Arcades, and that made it harder for Arcades to 'turn over' machines and they slowed down buying new arcade machines. And that is what I feel led to the 'game market crash'.
>
> George Moses and Don Gladden were very much the heart of the Michigan Bally Users Group. And George even went as far as working with Bally to write the Basic Manual update when the update to the Basic cartridge was released. But George did not write the music 'player', he used my music code, and wrote his music programs based on that. George was not a machine language programmer... Scott Noris was the person that programmed the 'music maker' cartridge.
>
> Before there was a "ZGRASS VIPER", there was a Datamax UV-1 ZGRASS machine that was used by Bally for game development (both for the home arcade, and their commercial games. I used on briefly.
>
> Anyway, interesting how history sees the old Bally/Astrocade days. It was a different thing all together to live through it... ;-)

Any lawsuits were simply done when the hobbyists crossed the line and it became a piracy problem, that is when a hobbyist tried to make enough money that it cut into the profits of the big guys.
